lesson_title: Your Car Door Zap Is Mini Lightning
hook_text: That sting when you touch a car door and a bolt of Highveld lightning are the same thing. One is just a few billion times bigger.
clip_script: You slide out of a car, touch the door, zap. Sliding across the seat charged your body. Air is normally an insulator, but with enough charge, about thirty thousand volts for every centimetre, it gives way. A narrow path of air becomes a conductor, charge rushes across, and the air glows and cracks. That is a spark. Now scale it up. In a summer storm cloud over Gauteng, ice bits crash together and the bottom of the cloud becomes hugely negative. A faint zigzag path creeps down, a streamer rises from a tall tree, they meet, and thirty thousand amperes surge through a channel hotter than the surface of the Sun. The air explodes outward: thunder. Count the seconds to the thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres. Hear thunder? Get inside a building or a metal car, and never under a tree.
visual_style: A whiteboard finger and car door with a tiny spark, then a zoom-out to a towering cloud with charges separating, a branching leader, and a flash, then a stopwatch counting seconds.
mood: Electric and dramatic, ending with practical safety.
pacing: A quick zap, a big build-up to the strike, then crisp safety rules.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to stay safe in a storm.
